topic: Linear Transformations and Matrices: The Geometry of Change

sections.title: Intuition: Transformations as Geometric Movement
sections.content: Define a linear transformation as a function that maps vectors to vectors, preserving grid lines (parallel remains parallel) and keeping the origin fixed.
sections.example: Imagine a digital 'Cat' character on a 2D plane. A transformation stretches, rotates, or shears the cat while ensuring its whiskers (vectors) remain connected to the origin.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Basis Vectors
sections.content: Explain that any 2D vector [x, y] is just a combination of basis vectors i-hat [1, 0] and j-hat [0, 1]. The transformation is defined entirely by where these two vectors land.
sections.example: Visualize a grid with two unit arrows. When we 'transform' the space, we track only where these two specific arrows point after the move.

sections.title: The Matrix: Encoding the Transformation
sections.content: Introduce the matrix as a concise container. The columns of the matrix represent the new coordinates of i-hat and j-hat. Matrix-vector multiplication is simply applying this change to any input vector.
sections.example: If i-hat moves to [1, 2] and j-hat moves to [-1, 1], the matrix is [[1, -1], [2, 1]]. Multiply this by a vector [3, 2] to see where the 'Cat''s foot lands.

sections.title: Synthesis: Application in Computer Graphics
sections.content: Summarize how matrices allow us to perform complex operations (rotations/scaling) by simple multiplication, forming the backbone of video game engines and animation.
sections.example: Show a 2D robot character spinning: each frame is just the robot's current position matrix multiplied by a 'rotation' matrix.
